chapter_title: The Case of the Fifth Word (Mystery and Magic)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 7 periods = 315 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 5h 15min

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Enter the World of Encyclopedia Brown

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.101): pre-reading crossword and multiple meanings of 'case'.
Let us discuss (p.104): complete four sentence stems with reasons.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the story's world through the pre-reading anagram crossword and the 'case' matching activity at 'Let us read' (p.101), inviting students to call out solutions aloud. This activates word-play awareness and primes the mystery context.

Teacher reads the story aloud (p.101–108) at an unhurried pace while students follow in their textbooks, pausing briefly at the moment Chief Brown shares the cryptic four words so students can hear the puzzle land. Students note unfamiliar words as the reading proceeds.

Students work in pairs on the 'Let us discuss' sentence-completion activity (p.104), filling in reasons for Leroy's nickname, Chief Brown's distracted dinner behaviour, Leroy's quiet observation, and Nolan's will. Pairs share answers for whole-class discussion.

Teacher draws the unit to a close by asking one open question: what kind of person do students picture Leroy to be from what they have read so far? Two or three quick responses are heard and the textbook is closed.

periods.teacher_notes: The pre-reading activities build two strands simultaneously — wordplay alertness (relevant to the code at the story's heart) and the flexible meaning of 'case' (detective case, pencil case, legal case). A common misreading at this stage is to treat the sentence-completion task as fill-in-the-blank rather than as reasoned explanation; nudge students to say why, not just what.

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Facts, Opinions, and the Character of a Detective

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.107): identify eight statements as fact or opinion.
Let us discuss (p.108): complete character-traits table for Leroy.
Let us think and reflect (p.109): Extract 1 — four questions on Chief Brown's dilemma and Leroy's modesty.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.104): reflect on whether Chief Brown would need Leroy's help and write two reasons.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the fact-versus-opinion distinction with one clear example from daily life, then students work individually on the eight-statement task at 'Let us think and reflect' (p.107). Verdicts are shared one by one and contested claims are discussed as a class.

Students complete the character-traits matching table at 'Let us discuss' (p.108), pairing textual evidence with traits such as humble, clever, and keen listener. A brief whole-class discussion draws out how the author shows rather than tells character.

Teacher reads Extract 1 aloud (p.109) — the passage about Chief Brown's pride and Leroy's silence — and students tackle the four follow-up questions: completing a sentence about Chief Brown's unique dilemma, the inference MCQ on why Leroy stays silent, the MCQ on the parents' naming choice, and the short-answer on being 'stuck with' a nickname.
Teacher takes a quick show of hands: do students admire Leroy's choice to stay ordinary, or do they think he should share his gift? One or two brief responses bring the discussion to a natural rest.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the story's opening and Leroy's quiet dinner-table role, students are now ready to read more critically — separating what the text states as fact from what characters or narrators assert as opinion. A common confusion is labelling Chief Brown's pride as a fact because it is described in the text; help students see that the narrator's positive framing is evaluative, not verifiable.

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Cracking the Code, then Sharpening the Ear

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.109–110): Extract 2 — four questions on the coded words and Mrs. Brown's attempt.
Let us listen (p.117): mark four statements true or false after hearing the observation-skills podcast.
Let us listen (p.117): fill five blanks with exact words from a second hearing.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Extract 2 aloud (p.109–110) — Chief Brown's puzzled head-shake and Mrs. Brown's partial decoding of 'Nom Utes Sweden Hurts' — and students work through the four questions: the MCQ on Chief Brown's reaction, the true/false on Mrs. Brown's approach, the short-answer on what her failure reveals, and the MCQ on Encyclopedia's purpose in redirecting the discussion.

Teacher reads the observation-skills podcast transcript aloud at a steady, natural pace while students listen and mark the four statements at 'Let us listen' (p.117) as true or false. Answers are checked immediately with a brief explanation of any wrong verdict.

Teacher reads the transcript a second time, slightly more slowly, while students fill the five sentence blanks at 'Let us listen' (p.117) with exact words or short phrases from the podcast. Partners compare answers before the teacher confirms each blank.

Teacher draws a quick link between the story and the podcast: Leroy's ability to crack the code relied on precisely the observation skills just discussed — slowing down, asking questions, noticing patterns. Students name one tip from the podcast that fits Leroy's method.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through the story's central puzzle in earlier reading, students now encounter the extract where both adults fail to crack the code — a productive point to discuss why lateral thinking differs from literal reading. For the listening task, students at this stage often paraphrase rather than use exact transcript words; remind them the task asks for precise phrasing they hear, not restatements.

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Pronunciation Practice and Mystery Group Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.117): practise pronunciation of tricky words from the text.
Let us speak (p.117): group discussion on 'The Interesting Aspects of a Mystery Story'.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the pronunciation of 'jewellery', 'clerk', and 'dessert' using the bracketed guides at 'Let us speak' (p.117), then leads the class through the extended practice list — January, sour, pizza, Wednesday, bowl, buffet, pronunciation — with students repeating in unison and then individually.

Teacher explains the group-discussion format: roles of moderator and speakers, the polite turn-taking phrases provided in the textbook, and the rule that the moderator ensures equal participation and closes with a summary. Groups of five or six are formed.

Groups conduct their discussion on 'The Interesting Aspects of a Mystery Story' at 'Let us speak' (p.117), using the textbook's agreement and disagreement phrases. Teacher circulates, nudging quieter members to contribute and reminding moderators to manage the floor.
One or two moderators share a brief summary of their group's key points with the whole class. Teacher gives a short feedback on fluency, use of the polite phrases, and group management.

periods.teacher_notes: The pronunciation activity is most effective when students see and say the words in the story's context — connecting 'dessert' to the dinner-table scene, for instance, prevents the common swap with 'desert'. During the group discussion, some students may default to retelling the plot rather than analysing what makes mystery stories interesting; steer them toward aspects such as suspense, coded clues, and character revelation.

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Report Writing: The Inter-school Art Exhibition

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.117): write a report on an inter-school art exhibition using the sample format.

time_bands.activity: Teacher walks through the sample football-tournament report at 'Let us write' (p.117), naming each structural element on the board: title with byline, opening paragraph covering what/who/when/where, two body paragraphs with sequence markers, and a closing paragraph on prize-giving. Students annotate the sample in their textbooks.

Class brainstorms together: what would be included in a report on an inter-school art exhibition — types of artwork displayed, participating schools, judges, prize ceremony, notable moments? Teacher notes eight to ten content points on the board as raw material students can draw on.

Students draft their report individually, using the four-paragraph structure and the sequence markers identified earlier. Teacher circulates, prompting students who stall on the opening sentence and checking that bylines and titles are included.

Students exchange their draft with a neighbour for a quick peer read, checking that all four structural sections are present and that at least two sequence markers appear in the body. One volunteer reads their opening paragraph aloud before the class closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The sample report on the football tournament provides a transferable template; help students see that the format stays constant while the content shifts to art. A frequent weakness at this stage is an opening paragraph that names the event but omits the when and where; flag this explicitly during the brainstorm. The draft, peer review, and any further revision all happen within this sitting.
materials: Textbook (p.117 — sample report and writing prompt)
Lined writing paper or exercise book

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Phrasal Verbs, Homophones, Word Puzzles, and Reported Questions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.111): match phrasal verbs from the text with meanings, then fill blanks.
Let us learn (p.111–112): fill blanks with correct homophone pairs.
Let us learn (p.113): fill blanks with relative/subordinating conjunctions in a detective-story paragraph.
Let us learn (p.115): transform five direct questions to reported speech using supplied frames.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.116): rewrite six sentences in reported speech independently.

time_bands.activity: Students match six phrasal verbs from the story — 'put on', 'cooled down', 'turned up', 'make of', 'figure out', 'got away with' — with their meanings at 'Let us learn' (p.111), then fill the six blanks using the correct phrasal verb. Teacher confirms answers and highlights how these verbs appear in the story's narrative.

Teacher introduces the five homophone pairs (week/weak, dying/dyeing, fore/four, peace/piece, break/brake) at 'Let us learn' (p.111–112) with a brief meaning clarification for each, then students fill the five sentence blanks individually. Pairs check each other's answers.

Students read the detective-story cloze paragraph at 'Let us learn' (p.113) and fill the eight blanks with relative and subordinating conjunctions from the supplied box, drawing on the story's own example sentences. Teacher reviews answers, explaining why each conjunction fits its clause.

Teacher models the direct-to-reported-speech transformation rules on the board — tense shift, pronoun change, question word order — then students complete the five reported-question frames at 'Let us learn' (p.115). Three students read their answers aloud; errors are corrected collaboratively.

periods.teacher_notes: The vocabulary-grammar work in this sitting draws directly from the story's language: phrasal verbs appeared in the narrative, and the interrogative sentences transformed into reported speech are Mrs. Brown's questions at the dinner table. Students frequently forget to change the word order inside reported Wh-questions (keeping it as a direct-question inversion); make the correct form visible on the board throughout the transformation practice. Students are asked to rewrite six further sentences in reported speech as independent practice after class.

periods.section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
periods.activity_title: Optical Illusions, Mystery Objects, and the World of Reference Books

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.117): examine optical illusions and share two-image observations with class.
Let us explore (p.117): play 'Name the Mystery Object' — teams prepare and guess with three hints.
Let us explore (p.117): choose five words and find their thesaurus alternatives; share with class.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.117): visit the library, examine an encyclopedia, and note how it differs from a dictionary.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays or distributes the optical-illusion images at 'Let us explore' (p.117) and gives students a brief quiet moment to observe each one individually before sharing what two things they see. The class discusses how perception works — connecting the idea to the way Leroy sees pattern where others see nonsense.

Teams of four or five play 'Name the Mystery Object' at 'Let us explore' (p.117): each team selects a classroom or everyday object, prepares three hints in writing (two minutes), then delivers the hints one at a time to rival teams who bid for points. Teacher tracks scores and coaches teams to make hints precise but not instantly revealing.

Students work individually with a classroom or personal thesaurus — or a shared digital tool — to find alternative words for five words of their choice at 'Let us explore' (p.117). Three or four students share a word and its alternatives; the class votes on which synonym fits the story's context best.

Teacher briefly explains what an encyclopedia is and how it differs from a dictionary, using Leroy's nickname as the hook, and sets the library visit from 'Let us explore' (p.117) as an independent task to carry out outside class.

periods.teacher_notes: The optical-illusion activity extends the story's central theme — seeing what others miss — into a perceptual experience students can feel directly. The mystery-object game asks students to practise precision of language: a vague hint gives away too little and bores the guesser, while an overly specific hint collapses the game; coach teams to calibrate. Students are directed to visit the library and compare an encyclopedia with a dictionary as an independent follow-up task.
materials: Textbook (p.117 — optical illusions and game instructions)
Thesaurus (print copies or classroom device access)

items.source_section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
items.source_lo: Student reads and analyses a prose narrative to distinguish factual evidence from opinion and to make character inferences using textual support.
items.source_context: Encyclopedia Brown's crime-solving at the dinner table; the coded four-word clue and character traits of Leroy, Chief Brown, and Mrs. Brown.
items.item_stem:
Read the following statements about the story 'The Case of the Fifth Word'. Decide whether each statement is a FACT (something that can be verified in the text) or an OPINION (a judgement or belief).
1. Leroy Brown's father was the head of the Idaville Police Department.
2. The Diamond Mart robbery took place five years before the events of the story.
3. Chief Brown must have been the cleverest police chief in the entire country.
4. The stolen jewellery from the Diamond Mart was never recovered before Leroy solved the case.

options.text: Chief Brown must have been the cleverest police chief in the entire country.
Leroy Brown's father was the head of the Idaville Police Department.
The Diamond Mart robbery took place five years before the events of the story.
The stolen jewellery from the Diamond Mart was never recovered before Leroy solved the case.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Fact — the text states that Chief Brown is head of the Idaville Police Department. 2. Fact — the text places the Diamond Mart heist five years before the story's events. 3. Opinion — this is an evaluative judgement by characters or the narrator, not a verifiable claim. 4. Fact — the text confirms no stolen jewellery was found before Leroy's deduction.

items.source_section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
items.source_lo: Student reads and analyses a prose narrative to distinguish factual evidence from opinion and to make character inferences using textual support.
items.source_context: Encyclopedia Brown's crime-solving at the dinner table; the coded four-word clue and character traits of Leroy, Chief Brown, and Mrs. Brown.
items.item_stem: In the story, Leroy never boasted about solving his father's cases, and Chief Brown never told anyone who his real detective was. Using specific details from the narrative — such as Leroy's behaviour at the dinner table, Chief Brown's silence about his son, and Leroy's one carefully chosen question about the fir tree — analyse what these choices reveal about each character. What does this shared secrecy suggest about the relationship between father and son?

expected_elements: Leroy's silence shows humility and desire to seem ordinary.
Chief Brown's silence reflects pride mixed with disbelief others would accept the truth.
Leroy's precise single question reveals disciplined, lateral thinking.
Their shared secrecy shows mutual respect and a protective, trusting bond.

items.source_section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
items.source_lo: Student listens critically to an informational podcast to distinguish accurate claims from inaccurate ones and to retrieve precise language from spoken text.
items.source_context: Podcast on five strategies to improve observation skills: slow down, engage senses, ask questions, take notes, practise mindfulness.
items.item_stem:
Your teacher will read the podcast on improving observation skills. As you listen, decide whether each statement below is TRUE or FALSE according to what is said in the podcast.
1. Taking time to focus on what is in front of you makes details clearer.
2. Observation is primarily about using the sense of sight rather than other senses.
3. Writing down or sketching what you observe can reinforce details in your memory.
4. Mindfulness helps a person stay present and fully engage with their surroundings.

options.text: Mindfulness helps a person stay present and fully engage with their surroundings.
Observation is primarily about using the sense of sight rather than other senses.
Taking time to focus on what is in front of you makes details clearer.
Writing down or sketching what you observe can reinforce details in your memory.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. True — the podcast says pausing to observe makes details become clearer. 2. False — the podcast explicitly states that observation is not just about seeing; it involves hearing, smelling, touching, and tasting. 3. True — the podcast says writing notes or quick sketches reinforces details in memory. 4. True — the podcast states mindfulness helps one stay present and fully engage with surroundings.

items.source_section_title: The Case of the Fifth Word
items.source_lo: Student listens critically to an informational podcast to distinguish accurate claims from inaccurate ones and to retrieve precise language from spoken text.
items.source_context: Podcast on five strategies to improve observation skills: slow down, engage senses, ask questions, take notes, practise mindfulness.
items.item_stem:
Your teacher will read the observation-skills podcast aloud. As you listen, complete each sentence below using one to three words exactly as you hear them in the podcast.
(a) Rushing through tasks often leads to _____________ that you might otherwise have noticed.
(b) The more senses you engage, the more _____________ you absorb.
(c) Curious people tend to be better observers because they actively try to _____________ what they are noticing.
(d) Even quick sketches of an object or place can strengthen your understanding of its _____________.

items.item_stem: In a group of four or five, take turns to describe what you find most gripping about a mystery story you have read or heard — this could include suspense, hidden clues, or surprising endings. Each speaker must build on what the previous speaker said, using a polite phrase such as 'I agree with what was said, and I would also add…' or 'I see it differently because…'. The moderator opens and closes the discussion with a brief summary.

expected_elements: Identifies a specific aspect of a mystery story with a brief reason.
Uses at least one polite agreement or disagreement phrase.
Responds to or builds on a previous speaker's point.
Speaks clearly enough to be heard across a small group.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are Leroy Brown's classmate. A visitor to your school asks you: 'What is it about Leroy that makes him such an unusual detective?' Play the role of the classmate and respond in two or three sentences, giving your opinion with at least one specific reason drawn from what you know of Leroy's character and methods.

expected_elements: States an opinion about Leroy's distinctive quality with a reason.
Uses a specific detail (e.g., asking one precise question, his vast reading, his modesty).
Speaks in the role of a classmate, not as a narrator summarising the story.
Uses at least one evaluative phrase ('I think', 'What strikes me is', 'In my view').

expected_elements: Title and byline present at the top of the report.
Opening paragraph answers what, who, when, and where.
Body uses at least two sequence markers to order events logically.
Closing paragraph includes a quote or remark from an authority figure.

items.source_context: Writing a report on an inter-school art exhibition using the sample football-tournament report as a format guide.
items.item_stem: Leroy Brown solves the mystery by noticing a pattern that everyone else missed. Imagine you are a journalist who has just learned how the stolen jewellery was recovered from the fir tree's jug of earth at Nolan's nursery. Write a short newspaper report (about 120 words) covering the discovery. You are free to choose what you include, but your report must have a headline, make clear what was found and where, and convey why the discovery is remarkable.

expected_elements: Headline captures the discovery in a striking, newsworthy phrase.
Report identifies the location (Nolan's nursery), the hiding place (fir tree jug), and what was recovered.
Explains or implies the coded-words method without needing to reproduce the full solution.
Conveys the significance or surprise of the find in the writer's own words.

items.item_stem: Match each phrasal verb from Column A with its correct meaning from Column B. The phrasal verbs are drawn from the story about Encyclopedia Brown.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A — Phrasal Verb | Column B — Meaning
figure out | appeared or been discovered
turned up | solve a problem or understand something
got away with | became calm or returned to normal
cooled down | escaped without being punished
make of | have an idea or understanding of something

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: figure out — solve a problem or understand something; turned up — appeared or been discovered; got away with — escaped without being punished; cooled down — became calm or returned to normal; make of — have an idea or understanding of something.

answer_key.right: solve a problem or understand something
became calm or returned to normal
have an idea or understanding of something

items.item_stem:
At the dinner table, Mrs. Brown asked several questions as the family tried to decode Nolan's message. Rewrite the following sentences, changing them from direct speech to reported speech. Make all necessary changes to tense, pronouns, and word order.
(a) Mrs. Brown asked Leroy, 'Can you figure out what these words mean?'
(b) Mrs. Brown asked Chief Brown, 'Did Davenport ever come back to collect the jewellery?'
(c) Mrs. Brown inquired, 'Where exactly did the officers find the document?'

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (a) Mrs. Brown asked Leroy whether he could figure out what those words meant. (b) Mrs. Brown asked Chief Brown whether Davenport had ever come back to collect the jewellery. (c) Mrs. Brown inquired where exactly the officers had found the document.

items.item_stem: Think about the 'Name the Mystery Object' game. Choose any object that could be found in a school — it could be something in your classroom, library, or science lab. Write three hints for it in order from the least revealing (Hint 1, worth 20 points) to the most revealing (Hint 3, worth 5 points). Each hint must be a complete sentence and must not name the object directly.

expected_elements: Three hints written in decreasing order of difficulty.
Each hint is a complete sentence that does not name the object.
Hints progress logically: broadest clue first, most specific last.
Language is precise enough to narrow the object without revealing it instantly.

items.source_context: Optical illusions; 'Name the Mystery Object' language game with three-hint structure; thesaurus exploration for five chosen words.
items.item_stem: Design a short language-and-observation project inspired by the chapter. Your project should have two parts: (1) Create your own simple word puzzle or coded message — similar in spirit to Nolan's four-word code — that a classmate could decode using pattern recognition. Explain the rule or pattern your code uses. (2) Use a thesaurus to find three alternative words for the word 'clever' and write one sentence for each alternative that shows its meaning in a situation involving observation or detection. Present both parts in a way a classmate could read and enjoy.

expected_elements: Word puzzle or code is original and its rule is clearly explained.
Three thesaurus alternatives for 'clever' are correctly identified.
Each sentence uses the alternative word meaningfully in a detection context.
Presentation is organised so a reader can follow both parts without guidance.
